# Control

## Types A and B

Digit 3 of an instruction divides them. An instruction of type A asks the
arithmetic part to do something (types K to T), and the next instruction is
the next in the table. An instruction of type B does nothing but name the
next one:

```
Instruction 491. A. Multiply the content of TS 23 by the content of TS 24
and store the result in TS 25. Then proceed to carry out the next
instruction (i.e. No. 492).

Instruction 492. B. Proceed with instruction 301.
```

In popular form a B is written `B, ` and the name of the instruction:
`B, ECHO 3`. Type B also leaves the position it came from in TS 1.

## Numbering

Section 7 describes how the tables of a job become machine form. The cards
of every table used are copied, sorted by the popular name and the detail
figure, and numbered consecutively; then every instruction that names
another has the number filled in. `ace` does the same, and the tables lie in
the delay lines in alphabetical order:

```console
$ ace tables examples/countdown.ace --emit listing

    3   DL 47,23   0000,1000,0110,0100,0000,0001,0000,0000   ADD 'A'
    4   DL 47,25   0000,0101,0000,0000,0010,1100,0011,0000   UNBURY 40 - TS 6
    5   DL 47,27   0000,0011,0010,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000   TS 6 - TS 2
    6   DL 47,29   0000,1000,0000,0100,0000,0001,0000,0000   SUBTRACT
    7   DL 47,31   0000,0010,0001,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000   TS 4 - TS 6
    8   DL 48,1    0000,0011,0111,1100,0000,0000,0000,0000   TS 6 - TS 31
    9   DL 48,3    0000,0101,0000,0000,0001,1100,0011,0000   UNBURY 41 - TS 6
   10   DL 48,5    0000,0011,0010,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000   TS 6 - TS 2
   11   DL 48,7    0000,1000,0100,0100,0000,0001,0000,0000   ADD
   12   DL 48,9    0000,0010,0001,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000   TS 4 - TS 6
   13   DL 48,11   0110,0000,0000,0000,1010,1000,0011,0000   B, 1, UNBURY 13
   14   DL 48,13   0000,0011,0010,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000   TS 6 - TS 2
   15   DL 48,15   0000,1000,0110,0100,0000,0001,0000,0000   ADD 'A'
   16   DL 48,17   0000,0101,0000,0000,0011,1100,0011,0000   UNBURY 42 - TS 6
   17   DL 48,19   0000,0011,0010,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000   TS 6 - TS 2
   18   DL 48,21   0000,1000,0100,0100,0000,0001,0000,0000   ADD
   19   DL 48,23   0000,0010,0001,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000   TS 4 - TS 6
   20   DL 48,25   0110,0000,0000,0000,1000,1100,0011,0000   B, 1, UNBURY 20
   40   DL 48,27   0000,0000,0000,0000,0100,0000,0000,0000   P, DL 0
   41   DL 48,29   0000,0101,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000   DL 0,1 - TS 6
   42   DL 48,31   0110,0000,0000,0000,0010,0000,0000,0000   B, DL 0,3
```

Consecutive instructions are two minor cycles apart: DL 32,1, DL 32,3,
DL 32,5. Chapter 10 says why.

## Detail figures

The number in front of an instruction is its detail figure. It may be left
out, and then the instruction is the one after the last. Writing it is a
check: `ace check` warns when it is not what counting gives. A number after
an instruction of type A, as INDEXIN has, is the number of the next
instruction, and is checked the same way. Figures may skip forwards, which
leaves room for instructions to be added, as Turing's CALPOL goes from 1 to
8 to 37.

## Obeying TS 6

A 1 in digit 17 of a B means: carry out the instruction in TS 6. If that is
of type A, the machine then goes on at the instruction after the B. So a
program can build an instruction and obey it:

```ace
MAKE
  1   Q, DL 7,1
  2   TS 6 - TS 9
  3   MAKE 20 - TS 10
  5   OR
  6   TS 8 - TS 6
  7   B, 1
  8   B, MAKE 8
 20   0000,0001,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000,0000

DL 7,1  +7
DL 7,2  +1
```

```output
7 1
```

Type Q puts digits 17 to 32 of the instruction, here the position DL 7,1,
into TS 6. OR adds the code of type O from MAKE 20, and `B, 1` obeys the
result: punch DL 7.

`B, 1, X` does the same and names X as well. INDEXIN 11 is written that way.
